title: IRDAI Exposure Draft Proposes Changes to Insurer Registration, Share-Transfer Thresholds, Mergers With Non-Insurance Holding Companies and Naming Rules
summary: IRDAI's exposure draft (comments until July 6, 2026) would let non-operative holding companies merge into their insurer subsidiaries, restructure share-transfer approval thresholds, allow foreign SPVs from FATF-compliant jurisdictions and reserve insurance-related names for insurers.
description:
India's insurance regulator has proposed a broad rewrite of the rules on who can own insurers and how they can be combined. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) released an exposure draft of the IRDAI (Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers) (First Amendment) Regulations, 2026. Public comments close on July 6, 2026, according to Business Standard and a client alert by the law firm Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, which analyses the draft. This article summarises the law firm's description of the proposals. An earlier version of this article said that the proposals included reduced transaction fees and followed India's move to allow 100% foreign investment. The analysis we reviewed does not mention fees or those links, so both points have been removed. These are proposals only; they take effect, if at all, after consultation and publication in the Official Gazette.

What is proposed for mergers? A new Regulation 30A would allow a non-insurance company to amalgamate with its insurer subsidiary if it is a non-operative holding company. It must hold more than 50% of the insurer's equity and have no business operations. The scheme would be prepared under Section 35 of the Insurance Act, 1938, and the insurer would be the surviving (transferee) entity. Consideration would be limited to the insurer's equity shares issued to the transferor's shareholders, with fractional entitlements paid in cash. Policyholders' funds could not be used for liabilities or obligations arising from the amalgamation, the insurer's solvency would have to stay above control level at all times, and after the merger the insurer could conduct only the insurance business it is registered for. Incoming shareholders would need to meet fit-and-proper criteria, a point the law firm says raises questions where shareholdings are dispersed or listed.

How would share-transfer approvals change? The draft would replace Regulation 21. For a holding of 5% or less, prior approval would still be needed if the holding is likely to exceed 5%. For a holding above 5%, prior approval would be needed whenever a transfer takes the holding past any 5% multiple, such as 10%, 15% or 20%. The previous rule was tied to each further 5% increase within a financial year. The threshold for shares transferred by a transferor would rise from 1% to 5% of paid-up equity capital per financial year. Intra-group transfers would expressly need prior approval. In a fresh issue, a pro-rata fall in a shareholder's holding from not subscribing would be treated as shares intended to be transferred. For listed insurers, the self-certification route for transfers of 1% to 5% in Regulation 25 would be omitted.

What about promoters and special purpose vehicles? The draft would allow a special purpose vehicle to be a promoter on satisfaction of the Authority, and delete the requirement for a valuation certificate from a SEBI-registered Category-I merchant banker, though the law firm argues it may survive through another provision. Fit-and-proper and minimum paid-up capital requirements would remain. Foreign promoters and foreign SPVs could be entities incorporated in a FATF-compliant jurisdiction. FATF is the Financial Action Task Force, the global body that sets standards against money laundering. The law firm notes that the term FATF-compliant jurisdiction is not defined and suggests a negative-list definition. It also notes the express exclusion of individuals from the foreign promoter definition is deleted, which creates ambiguity. Regulation 50 would codify a September 6, 2024 IRDAI circular allowing subscribers of other forms of capital to be entities from India or FATF-compliant jurisdictions.

What are the naming rules? A new Regulation 56A would reserve the words insurance, insurer, assurance, reinsurance, insurance company and derivatives for insurers, and require insurance businesses to use at least one such word. Existing insurers would have 12 months from notification to comply, and a no-objection certificate from the competent authority would be required for any name change.

What do the proposals mean? Supporters would likely see clearer thresholds and a path for holding company mergers as ease-of-doing-business reforms. Critics might worry about the effect on regulatory oversight of new owners and about how fit-and-proper tests apply to dispersed holdings. The law firm's alert raises several drafting questions, including undefined terms. We do not have the industry's responses, which are not yet public.

What should readers watch? The key dates are the July 6 comment deadline and the final regulations. Insurers, promoters and investors with holding company structures are most directly affected. Policyholders are not directly affected by the draft, and the proposed protection of policyholder funds in mergers is intended to keep it that way.

Because the law firm's alert is itself an interpretation, and because exposure drafts are often revised after comments, the details above may change before any rules are final.

This article summarises a draft regulation as described by a law firm and a news report. It is not legal advice, and readers should consult the exposure draft itself.
source_name: IRDAI exposure draft, as analysed by Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas and reported by Business Standard
image_alt: India insurance regulation and financial documents (illustrative)
key_points: The draft IRDAI (Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers) (First Amendment) Regulations, 2026 is open for public comments until July 6, 2026.

A new Regulation 30A would let a non-insurance company amalgamate with its insurer subsidiary if it is a non-operative holding company holding more than 50% of the insurer's equity, with the insurer as the surviving entity and policyholder funds protected.
Share transfers: holders above 5% would need prior approval whenever a transfer takes them past any 5% multiple, and the per-year threshold for shares transferred by a transferor rises from 1% to 5%.
Foreign promoters and special purpose vehicles could be entities from FATF-compliant jurisdictions, a term the draft does not define.
Only insurers could use 'insurance', 'insurer', 'assurance' or 'reinsurance' in their names, with existing insurers given 12 months to comply.
why_it_matters: These rules decide who can own and combine Indian insurers. Clearer thresholds could make restructurings easier, but they also raise questions about how well regulators can check the suitability of new owners.

title: Cowbell 2026 Cyber Claims Report: Ransomware Attacks Rose 45% in 2025 While Average Ransom Payments Fell About 44% Since 2022
summary: Cowbell's 2026 claims report, covered on May 7-8, 2026, says ransomware attacks rose 45% last year while average ransom payments fell roughly 44% between 2022 and 2025; data breaches, cybercrime and extortion drove most claims.
description:
Ransomware attacks went up in 2025, but the amounts paid to the attackers went down. That is the central finding of Cowbell's 2026 claims report, a cyber insurance claims analysis from the managing general agent Cowbell, as reported by Claims Journal in May 2026. According to the report, ransomware attacks rose 45% last year, while average ransom payments fell by roughly 44% between 2022 and 2025. This article summarises the Claims Journal coverage. An earlier version of this article described the figures as an industry-wide trend. They come from Cowbell's own claims data, so they reflect its portfolio and not the whole market, and the article now says so. Other figures sometimes quoted alongside this report, from Resilience and IBM X-Force, come from separate sources and are not part of the Cowbell report.

Why have payments fallen? Cowbell's director of claims, Stephanie Hewerdine, credits better negotiation, stronger claims handling and insureds' preparedness, including incident response plans and robust backups. In plain terms, if a business can restore its systems from backups, it has less reason to pay, and if it has a negotiator experienced in dealing with criminals, the sum agreed can be lower. The report's figure compares 2022 and 2025, so it describes a three-year trend and not a single year's change. The report as covered does not give the dollar amounts of average payments, so we cannot say what they were.

What are the claims about? In the past 18 months, according to the coverage, data breaches accounted for 33.5% of claims, cybercrime for 31.8% and extortion events for 18.3%. Together, those three categories make up about 84% of claims. Cybercrime in this context refers to financial crimes such as fraudulent funds transfers or business email compromise, though the coverage does not define each category in detail. The coverage also does not give claim severity figures, so we cannot say how large the average claim is.

How are attackers changing tactics? The report says extortion is shifting from encryption toward data-only schemes and double extortion. In a traditional ransomware attack, criminals encrypt a victim's files and demand payment for the key. In data-only extortion, they steal data and threaten to publish it. In double extortion, they do both. This shift matters because good backups, which can defeat encryption, do not stop a threat to publish stolen data. The report also says smaller, less sophisticated groups are emerging, and that some do not honour their agreements with victims. That makes negotiation riskier, because paying does not guarantee deletion of stolen data.

Who are the main threat actors? More than two-thirds of cases in which the attacker was identified involved seven groups. Akira accounted for 38.8% and Qilin for 14.2% of those cases, together more than half. The coverage does not describe how the groups operate, and this article does not add details beyond the report. Concentration among a few groups suggests that law enforcement action against one group could change the picture.

Which sectors are exposed? The report says that professional services, construction, manufacturing, healthcare and wholesale trade depend heavily on systems and sensitive data, which makes preparation especially important for them. It does not give claim rates by sector.

What should businesses do? The report's logic points to several practical steps: maintain tested, offline backups; keep an incident response plan and rehearse it; use multi-factor authentication and patching; and know whom to call, such as an insurer's breach coach, if an attack happens. Insurance does not prevent an attack, but it can pay for response, restoration and legal costs, depending on the policy. Policies differ on whether they cover ransom payments, and some regulators and governments restrict such payments. For instance, Germany's BaFin has confirmed that ransom payments can be insured under its rules, as covered separately on this site.

How does it fit the market? Munich Re and others have reported that global cyber insurance premiums are expected to soften in 2026 even as attack frequency rises, a theme covered elsewhere on this site. Cowbell's report suggests that insurers' claims experience can be better than frequency alone would suggest, if policyholders are prepared.

One more point is about interpretation. A rise of 45% in ransomware attacks sounds dramatic, but the report as covered does not give the underlying number of attacks or Cowbell's number of policyholders, so the percentage should be read as a trend within its book and not as an absolute measure. Similarly, the fall in average ransom payments may reflect changes in the mix of attackers and victims as well as better handling. Even so, the direction is encouraging for businesses that invest in preparation, and it fits with the logic that criminals have less leverage over a victim that can recover without them.

What about insurers? A falling average payment helps insurers if they cover ransoms, but rising attack frequency raises the number of claims for response, restoration and business interruption, which are separate from the ransom itself. Insurers therefore watch frequency, severity and the quality of customers' controls together, and many require minimum security measures before offering cover.

This article summarises one insurer's published claims analysis and is not insurance or security advice.
source_name: Cowbell 2026 Cyber Claims Report (via Claims Journal and Insurance Journal)
image_alt: Cybersecurity threat and ransomware cyber insurance claims data (illustrative)
key_points: Ransomware attacks rose 45% last year, while average ransom payments fell roughly 44% between 2022 and 2025.
Cowbell's director of claims, Stephanie Hewerdine, credits better negotiation, stronger claims handling and insureds' preparedness, including incident response plans and robust backups.
Over the past 18 months, data breaches were 33.5% of claims, cybercrime 31.8% and extortion events 18.3%.
Extortion is shifting from encryption toward data-only and double-extortion schemes; smaller, less sophisticated groups are emerging and some do not honour agreements with victims.

More than two-thirds of cases with identified actors involved seven groups, with Akira at 38.8% and Qilin at 14.2%; professional services, construction, manufacturing, healthcare and wholesale trade are especially exposed.
why_it_matters: Cyber attacks keep rising, but the report suggests that preparation and professional handling can cut the amount paid to criminals. That matters to any business deciding how much to invest in backups, response plans and insurance.

title: FCA Widens Scrutiny of Home and Travel Insurance After Which? Super-Complaint, Declines a Market Study and Promises an Update by End-2026
summary: The FCA's December 18, 2025 response to a Which? super-complaint accepts firms must do more under the Consumer Duty, will expand work on claims handling and sales processes, rejects a market study and will publish an update by the end of 2026.
description:
The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has agreed with part of a consumer group's complaint about home and travel insurance and is widening its work, but it has declined to launch a full market study. Which? submitted a super-complaint on September 23, 2025, arguing that insurance manufacturers and distributors show poor claims handling and inappropriate sales practices, and concluding that the FCA had failed its statutory objective to secure an appropriate degree of protection for consumers. The FCA published its response on December 18, 2025. This article summarises the FCA's response as described by the law firm HFW. An earlier version of this article described the FCA's expanded scrutiny as a development of 2026. The response was published in December 2025, and the work it describes continues through 2026, so the article now gives the dates. Our sources describe the response, not the detailed FCA document, and readers who need precise wording should consult the FCA's publication.

What did the FCA accept? The FCA accepts that complaints and claims-acceptance data show that firms must do more to meet the Consumer Duty in this area. The Consumer Duty is the regulator's standard requiring firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers. It points to existing work, including Guaranteed Asset Protection (GAP) insurance, support for the government's motor insurance taskforce, and an evaluation of pricing reforms that it found effective in reducing price-walking, which is the practice of charging loyal customers more at renewal. It also published a roadmap in July 2025.

What enforcement does it cite? The FCA cites two investigations launched, independent reviews of three firms' claims handling, feedback to major price comparison websites, and expanded analysis of sales processes. These are examples of action it says it has taken. The sources do not name the firms.

What will it expand? On claims handling and service quality, the FCA will review customer service, oversight of third-party claims handlers, and managing general agents, and widen this to delegated authority models, remuneration and conflicts. On customer understanding, it will analyse how different sales processes affect consumer outcomes. It identified two theories of harm: first, that sales and distribution processes limit consumers' ability to compare quality and suitability; second, that claims-handling incentives and supply chain arrangements reduce claims quality. The FCA will conduct focused analysis of the first issue, and handle the second through its existing work programme.

What did the FCA reject? It rejected Which?'s claim that it failed to enforce its rules and consumer law. It declined to run a market study at this stage. It will, however, consult in the first quarter of 2026 on reflecting the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act in its Handbook, and notes that it has already used powers under that Act to require unauthorised law firms to provide information on exit fees.

What happens next? The FCA says it will publish a public update on its actions by the end of 2026. That means the next significant information is expected after the period covered by this article. Insurers, brokers and price comparison sites should expect questions about how their sales processes explain cover and how their claims arrangements operate, especially where claims are handled by third parties.

What does this mean for consumers? The FCA's response does not change any policy, and it does not give consumers new rights directly. It signals priorities for the regulator's supervision, and firms that fall short could face action. Consumers with a complaint can go to the firm first and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service. They can also compare policies carefully, noting exclusions, excesses and limits, and keep records for any claim.

What does it mean for firms? The Consumer Duty applies to all parts of the distribution chain. The reference to managing general agents and delegated authority suggests that the FCA will look beyond the brand customers see to the firms that actually handle claims. Remuneration and conflicts of interest between distributors and claims handlers are named as areas of interest.

How does a super-complaint work? Under UK rules, designated consumer bodies such as Which? can ask the FCA to investigate features of a market that they believe significantly harm consumers. The regulator must respond publicly within a set period and say what it will do. The process does not force a particular outcome, but it puts the regulator's reasoning on the record, which is why the response is useful to read. In this case the FCA agreed on the problems with claims and sales, but chose to address them through supervision rather than a market study.

Why might the FCA have declined a market study? The sources do not give its full reasoning beyond saying it sees the issues as already within its work programme. A market study is a formal and lengthy exercise, and the regulator may judge that targeted supervision and enforcement will move faster. Which? and others may disagree, and may press for more action when the FCA publishes its update at the end of 2026.

This article summarises a regulator's response as reported by law and trade sources and is not legal advice.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority response to Which? super-complaint (as described by HFW)
image_alt: UK Financial Conduct Authority and insurance regulation (illustrative)
key_points: Which? submitted a super-complaint on September 23, 2025 arguing that home and travel insurance manufacturers and distributors show poor claims handling and inappropriate sales practices.
The FCA published its response on December 18, 2025, accepting that complaints and claims-acceptance data show firms must do more to meet the Consumer Duty.
It will expand work on claims handling and service quality, including oversight of third-party claims handlers and managing general agents, and analyse how sales processes affect consumer outcomes.
It rejected Which?'s claim that it failed to enforce its rules and declined to run a market study at this stage.
The FCA will conduct focused analysis of sales and distribution processes and publish a public update on its actions by the end of 2026.
why_it_matters: Home and travel insurance are bought by millions, and claims are where customers find out whether a policy works. The regulator's decision to widen its review shows what it expects insurers, brokers and comparison sites to fix.

title: BaFin's New Ransom Insurance Circular: Kidnapping, Cyber Extortion and Product Extortion Cover Allowed Under Strict Conditions
summary: BaFin's Circular 01/2026 (VA) on ransom insurance, reported on April 2, 2026, replaces a 1998 circular and confirms such cover is permissible if it respects public order and does not hinder law enforcement, with cyber-extortion cover now explicitly covered.
description:
Germany's financial supervisor has updated its rules on insurance against ransom demands, confirming that such cover is allowed if strict conditions are met. The Federal Financial Supervisory Authority, BaFin, issued Circular 01/2026 (VA) on ransom insurance. According to a report by cash-online.de dated April 2, 2026, the circular covers kidnapping, cyber extortion and product extortion. It replaces a circular from 1998, and consolidates the rules for the first time in nearly three decades. The substance is largely unchanged, but the structure is clearer. Commercial Risk reported on April 16, 2026, that BaFin confirmed that ransom payments to cybercriminals can be covered by insurance, either as standalone cover or as part of cyber policies. This article summarises these reports. An earlier version of this article said that BaFin separately flagged systemic accumulation risks in the cyber insurance market. The reports we reviewed do not mention that, so it has been removed. The circular text itself was not available to us, so this description relies on the reports.

What does the circular say about permissibility? According to the report, insurers may offer this cover under strict conditions. It must not violate public order, known in legal terms as ordre public, and it must not hinder law enforcement. The older 1998 circular, which we could read in BaFin's archive, made a similar point for kidnapping and product extortion: it said such insurance did not contravene public policy if confidentiality was preserved, police investigations were not hindered and collusion between perpetrators, victims and insurance staff was prevented. The 2026 circular carries this approach forward and extends it expressly to cyber extortion.

What are the conditions on sales and contracts? Advertising for ransom insurance is prohibited. Bundling it into all-in products is generally banned, with one exception: combination with cyber insurance. Policy terms are capped at one year, so that risk and asset positions are reassessed regularly. Insured sums must be proportionate to the customer's financial situation, since excessive sums could make the insured a more attractive target for extortion. Before a contract is concluded, a specialised security firm must advise the client and prepare an individual security concept. The reports do not say how this applies to cyber extortion, where the security concept may involve IT security advice.

What are the confidentiality rules? Policyholders may disclose the cover to a small circle, generally no more than three named trusted persons who must be bound to secrecy. Insurers must run contract administration through a central unit reporting directly to the board, encrypt data and apply strict confidentiality rules for staff. The reason is that if criminals know a victim has ransom cover, they may demand more, so secrecy is central to the product's design.

What happens after a claim? Crimes must be reported immediately, and insurers, policyholders and trusted persons must support investigators. The report states that quiet settlement without involving police is ruled out. This means that insurance cannot be used to pay criminals without informing the authorities, a point that is important for the debate over ransom payments.

What about annual reviews? At each renewal, policyholders must provide up-to-date information on their financial circumstances and risk factors. If they fail to do so on time, the contract ends automatically. This requirement fits with the one-year cap and the proportionality of the sum insured.

How does it relate to the wider debate? Governments and regulators around the world are discussing whether to restrict ransom payments, and whether insurance encourages them. The BaFin circular does not ban payments; it sets rules to keep insurance from undermining policing. Commercial Risk's subtitle notes that Google warned Germany is a hotspot for ransomware in Europe, though the excerpt we saw did not give details. For comparison, Cowbell's 2026 claims report, covered separately on this site, says ransomware attacks rose 45% in 2025 while average ransom payments fell about 44% since 2022, which suggests that preparation matters as much as insurance.

What does it mean for German businesses? Companies that want cyber extortion cover should ask insurers whether it is included in their cyber policy and under what conditions. They should be ready to share financial information at renewal, to keep the cover confidential, and to involve the police if an attack occurs. The reports describe ransom insurance as a niche product whose importance is growing alongside cyber risks.

Why have such conditions existed for so long? Kidnap and ransom insurance has historically been sensitive because critics argue it could increase the risk of kidnapping, or that payments fund crime. The supervisory approach, as the 1998 circular shows, was to allow the product but surround it with secrecy, proportionality and police involvement. The 2026 circular keeps that balance while bringing digital extortion within the same framework, which gives insurers and customers legal clarity about a type of cover that is growing in relevance.

What remains unclear? The reports do not say how the security-concept requirement works for cyber extortion, whether existing cyber policies need changes to comply, or whether BaFin will publish further guidance. Insurers will likely update their wording, and customers should ask about any changes at renewal.

This article summarises press reports of a supervisory circular and is not legal advice. Companies should read the circular and their policy wording.
source_name: BaFin Circular 01/2026 (VA), as reported by cash-online.de and Commercial Risk
image_alt: Cyber extortion and ransom insurance regulation in Germany (illustrative)
key_points: BaFin Circular 01/2026 (VA) covers kidnapping, cyber extortion and product extortion and replaces the 1998 circular, consolidating the rules for the first time in nearly three decades; the substance is largely unchanged.

Insurers may offer ransom cover under strict conditions: it must not violate public order or hinder law enforcement; advertising is prohibited and bundling is generally banned, except in combination with cyber insurance.
Policy terms are capped at one year, and insured sums must be proportionate to the customer's financial situation, since excessive sums could make the insured a more attractive extortion target.
Policyholders may disclose the cover to no more than three named trusted persons; insurers must administer contracts through a central unit reporting to the board with encrypted data.
Crimes must be reported to the police immediately and quiet settlement is ruled out; policyholders must update financial information at renewal or the contract ends automatically.
why_it_matters: Ransomware has made extortion insurance more relevant for businesses. Germany's supervisor has made clear that such cover can exist, but on tight conditions meant to avoid encouraging crime or undermining police work.

title: Michigan Supreme Court Backs Progressive's Rescission of an Auto Policy Over a Garaging Misstatement, Ruling Unanimously for the Insurer
summary: On April 20, 2026 the Michigan Supreme Court unanimously held that a trial court abused its discretion by reforming rather than rescinding a Progressive no-fault policy where the insured misstated where her cars were garaged.
description:
A mistake about where a car is kept can cost a driver their auto insurance, according to a unanimous decision of the Michigan Supreme Court. On April 20, 2026, the court ruled in a case brought by Janice Sherman against Progressive that a trial court had abused its discretion by reforming an auto policy instead of allowing the insurer to rescind it. The decision was reported on April 22 by Insurance Business, whose report this article summarises. An earlier version of this article described the case as one about driver misstatements in general. The court's decision is specifically about a misstatement of the garaging address, and the article now says so. This is a summary of a news report and not legal advice, and the formal opinion should be consulted for exact wording.

What were the facts? In November 2020, Janice Sherman bought a Michigan no-fault auto policy from Progressive covering a Cadillac and a Chrysler. Her application listed Clinton Township as her home address and as the garaging location, and identified herself as the sole resident and driver. She did not update the information when she renewed six months later. In July 2021, she was injured as a passenger in an insured vehicle when a hit-and-run driver struck it, and she filed a claim for personal protection insurance (PIP) benefits, the no-fault coverage that pays medical and related costs. Progressive's investigation found that the cars were garaged in Detroit, not Clinton Township. She lived in Detroit with her adult son, and one vehicle was garaged at her brother's home. None of this had been disclosed. Sherman said that her Detroit home was flooded and uninhabitable when she applied, that an agent completed the application, and that she never meant to defraud anyone. Progressive's underwriting specialist calculated that accurate information would have raised her premium by 83.2%.

What happened in the lower courts? Progressive denied the claim, rescinded the policy from the start, and refunded $1,491.54 in premiums. Sherman sued for benefits and breach of contract. The trial court denied Progressive's motion for summary disposition and ordered the policy reformed to a Detroit address, with Sherman required to repay the refund plus an additional premium, a total of $2,617.65. The Court of Appeals unanimously reversed. It held that the trial court erred in ordering reformation when the policyholder, not the insurer, engaged in misconduct. It vacated and reissued its opinion to clarify its reasoning, reaching the same result.

What did the Supreme Court decide? There were three holdings. First, on the standard of review, appellate courts reviewing a trial court's decision about rescission apply an abuse-of-discretion standard, not de novo review. This resolved confusion in lower courts, which had earlier applied a clear-error standard in a similar context. Second, the trial court abused its discretion, because the equities favoured Progressive: Sherman made material misrepresentations, Progressive relied on them, Progressive did nothing wrong, and no third-party interests were involved. Third, the court rejected Sherman's request for a new equities review by the trial court, distinguishing earlier cases where a remand was proper because no rescission analysis had been done. Six justices participated, and Justice Zahra wrote the opinion. Justice Noah Hood did not take part because he had sat on the Court of Appeals panel.

What does the ruling mean in practice? Under Michigan law, as described in the report, rescission is available when an applicant gives materially inaccurate information that the insurer relied on, regardless of intent. That means an honest mistake can still be material. The article stresses that rescission is not automatic: courts must weigh the equities, and the result could differ where the insurer's own conduct is at issue, for example where third parties such as an injured passenger's insurer or a medical provider have interests. The report does not identify a specific statute, and we do not name one.

Why does garaging matter? Insurers set rates partly by where a vehicle is kept, because theft, accident and claim costs differ by location. Michigan's auto market is known for high premiums in some areas. A difference of 83.2% in the premium, as Progressive calculated here, illustrates why insurers treat the address as material.

What should drivers do? Give accurate information about where each car is kept and who lives in the household, and update the insurer when circumstances change, including at renewal. If an agent completes an application, check it before signing. If something was wrong, correct it promptly. Misstatements can lead to rescission, denial of claims and loss of cover, which may be costly if injuries occur. Drivers with questions can ask their insurer or consult a lawyer or the state's insurance regulator.

This article is general information based on a news report of a court decision. It is not legal advice, and outcomes depend on the facts of each case.
source_name: Michigan Supreme Court opinion (April 20, 2026) as reported by Insurance Business and Beinsure
image_alt: Auto insurance policy and legal gavel representing court ruling on coverage (illustrative)
key_points: The Michigan Supreme Court decided Janice Sherman's case against Progressive on April 20, 2026, unanimously, in an opinion by Justice Brian K. Zahra; Justice Noah P. Hood did not participate.

Janice Sherman listed Clinton Township as her address and garaging location, but her cars were garaged in Detroit; Progressive's underwriter calculated accurate information would have raised her premium by 83.2%.

After a 2021 hit-and-run injury and PIP claim, Progressive denied the claim, rescinded the policy and refunded $1,491.54; the trial court reformed the policy to a Detroit address, but the Court of Appeals reversed.
The Supreme Court held that appellate review of a trial court's rescission decision is for abuse of discretion, and that the trial court abused it because the equities favoured Progressive.
Under Michigan law, rescission is available for materially inaccurate information the insurer relied on, regardless of intent, but it is not automatic: courts must weigh the equities.
why_it_matters: Where a car is garaged is a major rating factor in Michigan's expensive auto market. The ruling shows that a misstatement on an application can cost an injured insured their coverage, even if it was not intended to deceive.
